senses: A bird in the family Trogonidae from the order Trogoniformes, most of which live in Central and South America, have colorful feathers, and nest in holes in trees.
ety: Borrowed from translingual Trogon, from the present active participle of Ancient Greek τρώγω (trṓgō, “to chew, to gnaw”).

senses: Synonym of life; Biota; all living things.
A coniferous tree, Oriental arborvitae (Platycladus orientalis, syn. Biota orientalis).
ety: From New Latin biota, from Ancient Greek βιοτή (biotḗ), from βίος (bíos).

senses: A pattern morph of hognose snake that results in fewer but larger spots and often a completely black belly.
A hognose snake of this morph.
ety: Clipping of anaconda (“a morph of hognose snake”).

senses: The act of incinerating, or the state of being incinerated; cremation.
A spongy, flammable substance prepared from bracket fungi, formerly used as a styptic and as tinder.
ety: From French amadou (“tinder, lure, bait”), from amadouer (“to allure, caress”), perhaps from Icelandic mata (“to feed”), which is akin to English meat.

senses: Coarse grains produced at an intermediate stage of wheat flour milling.
Such grains, usually from durum wheat, used in the preparation of pasta, couscous and various sweet dishes.
ety: From earlier semolino, borrowed from Italian semolino, diminutive of semola, from Latin simila (“finest wheat flour”). Compare regional German Semmel (“bread roll”).

senses: A Japanese omelette made by rolling together several layers of cooked egg, usually prepared in a rectangular pan.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 卵焼き (literally “grilled egg”).

senses: A partner, assistant, or deputy.
examples: With the 2005 incarnation of Temptation, Livinia Nixon has completed the trifecta of TV seconds: variety offsider, game show hostess and weather girl.

senses: always, still; maintaining the same style
A knife for taking the hair off skins.
An infusion of pigeon's dung used by tanners to neutralize the effects of lime and give flexibility to skins; -- called also grains and bate.
One who grains (paints in imitation of the grain of wood, marble, etc).
A brush or tool used for such painting.
A grain car.
ety: From grain + -er. Piecewise doublet of corner.

senses: The belief that all truth is exclusively discovered through science.
ety: From scient- (in either Classical Latin scientia or scientific) + -ism. Compare scientist.

senses: One who is impaneled on a jury, or who serves as a juror.
A process, or projecting part.
Somewhat low.
examples: We climbed over a lowish fence to reach the meadow.

senses: To counteract the effects of previous programming or brainwashing, especially in an attempt to persuade (a person) to abandon allegiance to a cult.
Having a tab (protruding strip of material).
examples: Letter up a tabbed folder for each different catalog you intend to issue. As you collect matter for this catalog, put it in the one place — the folder devoted to that catalog.

senses: One who leans, or inclines toward something.
A vertical sign, usually leaned on a porch and made from repurposed wood.
Not pigmented.
A sociopolitical movement combining feminism and environmentalism.
Furnished with tines.
examples: And the Gray Men, with their eyes fixed upon their master, nodded all their hundred heads and put their hands upon the dangerous three-tined forks that were stuck in every one of the hundred belts.

senses: The comic actress in an opera.
ety: From Italian buffa. See buffo and buffoon.

senses: Someone in a team.
A player who teams with other players, often in an FFA match.
Synonym of ultrasonographer
A traditional Hawaiian cooking method, using an underground oven called an imu.
Having a ponytail.
examples: As he did so a couple walked in the door and mounted the platform: a young woman with a long dress and a snow white wig, and a ponytailed young man wearing a colonial soldier's cape and sword.
Gregarious, suntanned and ponytailed — as if he had just come in from the beach.

senses: Congenital lack of melanin pigmentation in the skin, eyes, and hair or feathers (or more rarely only in the eyes); the condition of being albino.
One who hocks or pawns an item.
Brutal, violent behaviour; savagery.
examples: Instances of misguidance like the ones given, and at least recognized in retrospect, in fascism, racism, and ecological brutalism, are also to be sensed by religious communication in other contexts.

senses: A stall; a fold for cattle.
A prop; a support, as for the feet in standing or climbing.
ety: Alteration of stall, after the verb to stell.

senses: A dish made from cattle's or sheep's head and/or trotters and eaten with garlic and/or vinegar.
A worker who separated the coarse part of flax or hemp with a hackle; a flax-dresser
A very fine, semi-opaque fabric similar to muslin, typically made of silk, wool or cotton.
A soft, light sweet or savoury mousse.
A hollandaise sauce that has been made frothy with whipped cream or egg white, served mainly with fish or asparagus.
A very thin glass for claret glasses.
ety: From French mousseline. Doublet of muslin.

senses: Any elevated object on land which serves as a guide to mariners, such as a hill or steeple.
A beacon, buoy, etc. placed in the sea to aid navigation.
A stew made from kernels of corn, lima beans, tomatoes and sometimes peppers.
ety: Borrowed from Narragansett msíckquatash (“boiled corn kernels”).

senses: That which decompresses.
To treat with a chromate solution
Something which rolls up other objects, growing increasingly large.
ety: From Japanese 固(かた)まり (katamari, “clump”), popularized by the 2004 video game Katamari Damacy and its sequels, in which players have to roll everyday objects into huge balls.
examples: Also, like a katamari, she tended to destroy things in her path. I would miss her. Hopefully marriage wouldn't change her too much.
It's like a Katamari effect. It would take only the slightest hint of a revolution to roll it all up.

senses: To deliberately act evasively or prolong a discussion in order to gain time or postpone a decision, sometimes so that a compromise can be reached or simply to make a conversation more temperate; to stall for time.
To discuss, to negotiate; to reach a compromise.
ety: From Middle French temporiser (“to wait one's time, temporize”) + English -ize (suffix forming verbs). Temporiser is derived from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin temporāre (“to delay, put off”) + -izāre (suffix forming the present active infinitive of verbs). Temporāre is derived from tempor-, the inflected stem of tempus (“age, time, period; season of the year; due, opportune, or proper time”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temp-, *ten- (“to extend, stretch (in the sense of a stretch of time)”), or *temh₁- (“to cut (in the sense of a section of time)”)) + -āre. Compare temporali

senses: To play a power chord on an electric guitar.
examples: Meanwhile, with Brain Stew, Green Day do some serious kerranging on their electric guitars, which they have mixed in with Godzilla vocals (!), to provide a tune of migraine-inducing proportions.

senses: Finely chopped.
Minutely subdivided.
Weakened, extenuated.
ety: From Middle English mynced, ymynced, y-mynsed. By surface analysis, mince + -ed.
